transcript.content: Got a great show. Uh, went shopping yesterday.
It's beautiful to have him back. I can't believe it.
Yeah. Wesley Willis, Rock and Roll Will Never Die. I'll be playing some of my favourites.
I don't know whether to play Hootie and the Blowfish, Kurt Cobain, Rolling Stones, Pink Floyd. They're all the same song.
It's interesting because, Gervais, you know, in the in the song that we've been on, we've had a lot of new listeners join us.
And they haven't perhaps heard Wesley Willis.
What a treat they've got in store.
Well, I'll explain that a little bit later. I've also, um...
Once again I was struggling, you know, as I, uh, don't plan the show, obviously.
But my book exchange in the in the courtyard of my house, it's come through again.
I've got a little book here.
Now, what was the last book you got from the book exchange?
Um, How to Beat PMT by Diet.
How to Beat PMT by Diet.
Which I could give away. I've got that at home. That would be a great prize one day.
A wonderful prize. A lot of women would look forward to that.
It's a little paperback here. Go on. Doris Stokes, Voices in My Ear.

The autobiography of a medium. A medium what? I don't, I don't know. But I've got to read you the bit off the back. You'll love this, okay? She's helped to solve murder cases. She filled the Sydney Opera House three nights in a row.
It doesn't say with what. Once, she even had to convince a man he was dead.
Now she's written her own astonishing life story. Her name is Doris Stokes. I'll be reading little excerpts from that.
Wait, I just, I mean, I don't know if you've read it, but why did she have to convince a man he was dead?
I don't know. It's in there.
I don't know. Well, that's just one of the little questions we'll be asking on XFM.

104.9, Ricky Gervais Show. I'm Ricky Gervais, and I've got Wesley Willis' as well, one of his some greatest LPs. I think he's actually recorded about 4,000 songs. Now, the thing is, this is quite true, he's a chronic schizophrenic and is often troubled by demons that dictate what he can do and what can't be done.
Uh, the de- demons sometimes prevent Wesley Willis travelling on airplanes, tell him that his music is no good and on occasion have forced him to destroy musical instruments. Now...
Can I just stop you there? I don't think it's demons telling him his music's no good. I think that's members of the public, anybody who's bought one of his albums.

Oh, and, um, he's, he's released fourteen CDs, um, by himself. He just makes them up and sells them. It's fantastic. This is, um, uh, the first track on Rock and Roll Will Never Die. It's called, um, Hootie and the Blowfish.
Wesley Willis - Hootie and the Blowfish
[Ricky and Steve sing along with the chorus.]
Um, after High Llamas, um, I'll- I'll play "Kurt Cobain."
That's, uh, Kurt Cobain. That's actually by, um, Wesley Willis.
Fantastic. Well, I'm gonna try and...
I think he's written a song about Nirvana as well.
Let me have a look on here. I've got, I've got the album here. Uh... No, I think it's, on this particular al— Oh no, you're right. No, Kurt Cobain is track two. Kurt, uh, track three is, uh, Nirvana.
Let's have, perhaps, a listen to that. Wonder if that's sort of different. I wonder what, what kind of, um, interpretation he gives to that particular band. I wonder how he sort of...
I don't know how to do this. I don't know how to work this machine.
You don't have to do it? Well, perhaps we should leave it, Gervais. Come back to it. Don't feel pressurised. I know we're keen to hear, Wesley.
Look, it won't let me do it.
There's no pressure on you. Gervais. I know you're getting a bit panicky now. I can see the sweat on your forehead.
Why doesn't it— why, why doesn't it do what I think?
Why do I have to actually press buttons and it doesn't know what I want?
No, but that's because, that's because you're not Doris Stokes, Gervais. You cannot use telekinesis to, to run this radio show.
Well, it would be, wouldn't it?
He gets about, mind. He sees a lot of gigs.
And he seems to know how many people are there.
To know how many people were there.
Well, um, it's, uh, twenty past four. It's the Ricky Gervais Show and, um, next is...
But, um, Steve, my chauffeur and researcher, you're meant to have found out why Doris Stokes had to convince a man he was dead.
Gervais, I've been looking through Voices in My Ear, the autobiography of Doris Stokes, the famous medium, and it I must say it's a fascinating read.
It's not a biography, and it's by someone.
Doris is too busy contacting the other side, Gervais.
Um, but, so basically, let me just answer that. Yeah, on the back it does say that once Doris had to convince a man he was dead. It's not as interesting as it sounds.
And she saw him, you know, and he wasn't... you see a big group of people, and he was like a ghostly figure. And he said, I'm not dead. She went, you are dead, get out.
You've had a similar argument with someone once, haven't you, at a dinner party?
Yeah, you proved her wrong, though, didn't you?
So he— she just— that, that happens a lot though. Some people don't believe they're— You know what it's like.
You go to the afterlife, no one tells you.
You're walking round. You're dead, mate. Don't be stupid. You know.
She had to actually push the coffin lid down, apparently. It's... a Viagra he died of.
I'm reading here about her, one of her first paranormal experiences.
She moved into a house with her husband. Um, there were ghostly apparitions there in the house, right, and it was haunted. She didn't mind. There was a, an old, an old ghost called Polly.
In the house. Lovely old ghost called Polly.

Anyway, so, um, uh, Mrs, uh, Johnson from nearby comes in and she's brought, uh, she's making a cake, basically. And, uh, she says, um, "We chatted for a moment. 'Any more trouble lately with the ghost?' said Mrs Johnson. 'No, old Polly's been quiet for, uh, for quite a while now.'"
But the words were hardly out of my mouth. When the bowl of eggs I was baking with...
...was torn from my hands and hurled across the room.
Instinctively, I dived after it, did a flying tackle...
...and caught it before it hit the ground. Now, I must say that Doris, at this point, has already lost a pair of tights.
Polly's already had a pair of tights.
Now the eggs are in danger.
You can just stop that, Polly, I yelled furiously and slammed the bowl of eggs on the table. She'd already cost me a pair of stockings. She wasn't spilling my eggs as well.
Oh, That's gotta be a euphemism. That's got to be a dirty book.
Doris Stokes there, fighting the paranormal.
You can't libel the dead to say what you want.
So we can slag off Doris Stokes?
You could say she drank buckets of, um... Just after the break, we've got Oasis.
You mean to tell me you can't libel the dead?
You can't libel the dead, no.
I don't believe that. For a moment.

It doesn't mean you can say— there's certain stuff you can't say anyway, whether it's true or not. It's taste and decency, and I, I couldn't— you couldn't say Doris Stokes drank copious amounts of horse spunk, 'cause you couldn't actually say that on the radio, 'cause that'd be offensive anyway.
But can I say, I mean, uh, Catherine Cookson died recently.
Can I say that Katherine Cookson used to bend over the sink and her husband would, I mean, can I...
Well... Again, taste and decency. I mean, you know, you couldn't be sued for it. Like, let's see, um, you could say Doris Stokes was a smackhead, for example.
She used to jack up all over the place.
And she used to, I mean, the trips she used to take.
All that nonsense about seeing and speaking to people on the other side. That's rubbish.
And you told me you don't swear.
No, that's all right. That's not swearing.
No. It's, er- it's an illegitimate child.
Oh, that's what you called that Steve.
Why- why did I say that? I can't remember.
Oh, I know, 'cause he- his uncle bought him summat and he told him he didn't like it.
Oh, yeah. And he didn't appreciate it.
Old- old bloke, he's got wooden teeth, apparently.
He's got wooden teeth. Oh, that's his granddad. His granddad's got wooden teeth or summat and he's got three left.
And he said they have to cook meat for about half- for eight hours, so he- so he can suck it.
I'd better start thinking of some, um, things that happened to Bob, hadn't I, so I can get him involved.
Well, he was a horrible little git.
I remember he had you up the hallway with Peter Miller teasing you and dropped you on your head.
I was dropped on my head when I was a kid. How old was I?
You must've only been two or three. Dropped you up the hallway.
I landed on my head, right? And what did I do? Was I unconscious or did I cry or...
No, you thought it was funny.
Good job I landed on me head, innit?
Are you going to continue to exploit your mother on the radio for cheap laughs?
That phone call, a lot of questions are raised.
The first one, obviously, that springs to mind, you were dropped on your head as a child.
It answers a lot of questions.
Gervais, you know, I— 'cause I did—
I don't even know who Peter Miller is.
Where is Peter Miller now? Who is he?
Let me be honest. Can I just be honest and confess something to you?
I have been making inquiries because I thought you had Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

I did. I thought you had CJD. I'm absolutely earnest and serious about this. Right? Because my dad once, we thought he might be ill. And we had checked over and it was terrible. It was a terrible moment. I felt sick.
And that's exactly what I felt like with you.
Um, no. But I did think you might have CJD.
And, um, I've been making enquiries.
The symptoms seem to be there. Gervais, you can barely string a sentence together. You're slovenly. Look at you. I mean, d'you know what I mean? You let yourself go.
You forget to wash. You forget to brush—
You stagger home every night. Yeah. You don't finish sentences.
You— d'you know what I mean? It's pointing in that direction.
So do you think I've got CDG, BSE, right? From the Agricultural College. Three BSEs. 0171580.

0171 580 2000. Please can somebody who knows about these things analyse Ricky Gervais's symptoms and find out— there's got to be something wrong with him. We think maybe now that he was dropped on his head as a child, that's perhaps a clue. If you're a medical person, if you've done some, uh, research into this, please give us a call.

Find out what's wrong with Gervais before it's too late. Perhaps it's, it— perhaps it is too late, Gervais. You know, you're not a young man anymore. You're thirty-seven plus. Um, you're, you're a goner. Um, and, so yeah, give us a call. 0171 580... Oh my God, it's catching.
Remember the tent you built out the back with—
Yeah. And I remember I didn't know... Didn't get it till I was 18 that Marsha had put the caption in the, um, photo album, Ricky's Camp.
You know I'm taping this, don't you?
Good job I ain't swearing then, ain't I?
You did. You said at the beginning. See, I'm going to take that out of context. It's just going to be you going, Bastard. Just like I've got you saying, Arse.
Listen to that, Muttley! Listen to that!
Oh, listen. Oh, I'm gonna shut up. Just laugh a minute. Just laugh.
You can't say that on the radio.
Stop it You can't swear on the radio.
I'm not saying what you think I'm saying.
Remember that time when you, we were coughing, and you coughed up that, and you killed next door's cat?
It was a little bit of hard lung that shot out. But they reckon—
Oh, I've never gone that far. You're disgusting.
All right, then. I'll see you later.

It really is. Your relations! I mean, all right, so my, my, you know, my, my, my relations, all right, their faces aren't symmetrical, but, but at least they don't have wheezy, weird laughs like that.
Yeah, I know, and drop people on their heads.

Right, I've got to tell you, I wish I was taping her, uh, uh, today. She called me today. She went, "Ain't heard of you for a while." I said, "I called you last week." "No, you didn't." I said, "Well, just bef— on Thursday." "Yeah. Anyway, I went swimming Wednesday." I went, "Did you?"
Where? She went In the fish pond?

Totally true. I thought— She went, "I fell in. It was up to me neck." And I could hear me nephew shouting, "It's only two foot deep!" Right? It's a little fish pond with a— it is. It's like about— it's not even two foot deep. It's about eight inches deep.
She went, well, I'm pissing myself. She's going, well, I was cutting back the lavender, right, and three frogs jumped at me.
I know she meant— Anyway, right, so—
Three Frenchmen hiding in your garden.
Yeah! No, yeah, that's what I was gonna say. I thought, no, that's a racial slur. Um, but anyway...
No, 'cause they— no, because French people—
Like to hide in lavender and fight in 73-year-old women.
Of course they do. Everybody knows that.
In stripy white, white and blue T-shirts and berets with onions.
I mean, I mean, I'll tell you, who is it, that pres— that dead president of France? What's his name? With the big nose.
Do you know what he used to do?
He used to drink bucketfuls of... Anyway, right?
You can do it 'cause he's, he's, he's dead. You can.
So, um, she went, "And I went in, and I fell in, and I was sitting on the bottom and it was coming up to me neck." And she went, "And I tried to get out, but it was all algae on the sides."
"I kept slipping back in," right? And my dad says, "Lee, help your nan!"

And she said, uh, "And I got out," and I, I said, "Put Lee on." I, I was speaking to me nephew. He said, "She went into the pond," right, and said she floundered around, right, and she got out and she walked— she ran to the kitchen, she—
And she dropped all her clothes and ran upstairs naked because she thought she might have leeches on.
She's not Humphrey Bogart in The African Queen.
She said, it wouldn't have mattered if it was aceful of company. I'd have still stripped off and run upstairs. She said, I didn't drop the scissors. And she said, I had to throw my slippers away.
So we're laughing at the fact that your elderly mother fell, slipped in a pond, could easily have injured herself quite seriously. Who knows? Now she could have leeches.
Yeah, she's probably got leeches. Yeah.
There was no sign of them. All they found was they just left a beret.
I'll tell you, the French, I mean, you know, any sign of, any sign of trouble, Gervais, they're out of there.
D'you know what I mean? They're legging it.
Oh, God. I just like the idea of her just running into the kitchen and stripping off, just a ball of slime, and then upstairs. "I couldn't wait to get in the bath," she said.
Yeah, and two ladies from next door, from the women's guild, just sipping tea. Oh, there she goes. There goes Mrs. Gervais. Naked as the day she was born, covered in algae.
Blood on the Tracks. And that was for, um, Doris Stokes.
The late, great medium Doris Stokes.
Who apparently, uh, Doris apparently was a prostitute.
You can't libel the dead. That's not libelous.
Um, yeah. She apparently went at it hammer and tongs.
With anybody that had a cheque.
Well, I've had a good eight months in radio, haven't I?
We've had a good, we've had—
We've had a bit of fun. I was gonna tell you about something, but what I'll do is I'll tell you in a minute.
How does he not run out of ideas?
It's incredible. They just flow from him.

It's incredible. Um, that, of course, comes from the classic Wesley Willis album, Rock and Roll Will Never Die. Just reading the sleeve notes, Gervais. And, um, Rock and Roll Will Never Die represents the best of Wesley's previously available material about rock musicians.
Um, his, uh, his quote, pers— his personal quote is, "This CD whoops the llama's ass with a belt." Not sure I know what that means, but anyway, apparently...
Hey, you can't libel the dead.
Wesley carries copies of his CDs with him when he travels, just in case he meets someone with $10 in their pocket.
Now that's a beautiful track. Track eight on that classic album. And of course, "Spin Doctors." Let's hear a bit more.
Beautiful. You see, he's a talented musician.
And "Kurt Cobain" and "Hootie and the Blowfish."
This one is, er, about the Spin Doctors.
Well, that's enough of that. That was for Laura, anyway, wrote me a lovely letter. Remember we, yes— yesterday, um, last week, sorry, I was going on about how we could do the best of Ricky Gervais?

So I could just, like, get bits off the login tape and package it and we wouldn't have to come in. We could, like, sunbathe or something. And she said, maybe you could do um, the best of Ricky Gervais, all the things that didn't happen.
All the things we said we were going to do, and then didn't. And.

And, uh, there are quite a few. There are quite a few. But she goes on as well, 'cause we were talking about reincarnation, and, um, she believes in that, um, uh, the, uh, Hindu view, um, of karma. So if, in, through your life, you do good things, you build up your good karma. Bad things, bad karma. Then when you die, they, they mount it all up, tot it all up, and you're reincarnated if you do, um, nice things.

It's a, a wonderful existence. Lovely, probably good looks, oh, everything. Everyone loves you. And if you're really bad, then you come back as something hideous like a maggot or a fish and you have a horrible life. And, um, the idea leads to, to wonder what you did that was so bad in your last life.
You're not baiting me. You're not baiting me.
Gervais, can I just say, I, you know, we've had some fun, we've had some laughs over the, uh, the last couple of months.
But I'm a little bit, I'm a little bit sick and annoyed about all this slagging me off, claiming that I'm some ugly, grotesque freak of nature or whatever.
Because, you know, we're getting loads of faxes coming in—
—saying, "Steve, you're a freak. You're, you know, you're an inhumanoid."

Um, and all this sort of rubbish. And, you know, it's not true, and you've just, you've perpetuated this myth for a long time and it's getting a bit irritating. It's winding me up. And I, as I've said to you before, um, I got into radio.
I got into this broadcasting thing, where the chances of becoming a celebrity are fairly strong. I got into this in an effort to meet women. To.
D'you know what I mean? And it's just, it's not helping me—
Well, I told you, you shouldn't pick careers based on whether you can get a woman.
Like the gynaecology thing. That's why that fell flat.
Yeah, but I— no, that was going all right. I mean, I overstepped a few times. You know, I just sort of mentioned— remember I mentioned to that woman that we should just go back and—
The first thing you say— exactly. And the other thing is, um, just saying, "Whey!" That doesn't put women at their ease.
Mrs. Johnson, would you mind just taking your clothes off?
Can I film this for the lads?
This is Happy Mondays. Yeah. Kinky Afro.
Would you just stop now with the...
Of course I will. You're a good-looking fella.
Oh, the classics, Gervais. I just got to thinking. I wonder if we... I mean, I think I mentioned this before. It'd be great to contact Wesley and get him to do a song about the Ricky Gervais show.
Well, you've pretty much done it for us.
Beautiful. Gervais, um, coming in on today...
[Imitating Wesley Willis] He had a radio show. There was about a hundred people listening.
Well, yeah. I think he's been a bit generous.

Gervais, um, I was on the Tube coming in and I got to thinking about, you know, my lack of success with the ladies. And I could trace it back to something. Or I traced it back to a moment. When, when I was in the, uh, the last year of my junior school. What, I don't know how old you'd be. How old?
11, something like that. We went to...
You were only about six foot two then, weren't you?
Yeah. And we, uh, we went to this sort of, um, place in Cornwall, sort of an adventure camp, you know. We stayed there for, like, three days.
That was like the Riviera to you, wasn't it?
Exciting stuff. And we had lots of, you know, there was all sort of climbing frames and, like, adventure courses and, you know, abseiling and all the rest of it.

And in the evening, what they'd do is you'd go in and they'd have, er, like a little disco. Every evening, a little disco, right? And, um, they- I remember they played, er, they played that tune, that theme music from, um, from, er-
Whatever that was called. No, it was, er-
Oh, Axel F. It was "Beverly Hills Cop," yeah.
And remember that one? It was, well, "We're Only Buggin'." [Sings] Ba-ba-ba-buggin', bug, bug-
Bug. It was that as well. That was a big tune. And also, er, "Living Doll" by Cliff.
Yeah, and, er, the Young Ones.

And we'd all queue up. Before we went on the dance floor, we'd all queue up and they'd give us little cups of soup. Dunno why. Little oxtail soup, I remember. It was quite nice. And then what happened was we, I don't know, we must've been a bit older, 'cause the guys—
Doris Stokes used to spike kids' soup to do with um, heroin.
That's true enough. That is absolutely true. You can't label the dead.

And, um, we must have been slightly older, because all the kids, all the guys, started to ask the girls, like, to dance with them, you know, cheek-to-cheek style. It was the first time that this had happened, you know. And suddenly I saw, like, girls and guys dancing together.
But I, instead of going, asking a girl to dance, you know, like any normal human being, every other bloke, every other, you know, guy was asking a girl to dance. I went round with a notepad,
I went round with a notepad pretending I was a brain surgeon.
I went round and said, I'm a brain surgeon. I want to analyse if you're mad so I can work surgery, do surgery on your brain. And I would ask them a series of questions.
Not just the girls, this was folks as well. While they were dancing. While they were dancing, you know, smooching or whatever, I'd go up to them.
What did you think this would achieve?
And say, can I ask you a series of questions? I'm a brain surgeon. And I thought it was funny. I thought it was charming.
I thought it was charming and funny and wacky.
And they were meant to go, "Oh, isn't that funny eleven-year-old freak, right, in the clogs and overalls, I wouldn't mind dancing with him."
I thought that, that kind of wit and zany charm would, uh, would somehow...
I'll stop you there, Steve, because you're boring me. After the break, some Beatles.
Doesn't. Doesn't help. Uh, Doris Stokes, right—
—onto the naked torso of Arthur Mullard.
Right, and, um, he in turn is being pleasured, right, by Dusty Springfield.
You twat. Dusty Springfield's not dead.
Of course she's not. You, you...
She's dead. Of course she's dead.
I don't know. Dusty Springfield's alive and well. And playing with Arthur Mullard. No, she's not dead.
Well, excellent. It was going so well, wasn't it?
I like the bit up until then, though.
I like the idea of her and Mullard.
...in a farm. We can't do that anyway, still, 'cause you can't do that on the radio, talking about that sort of thing.
I'll tell you what, though, if we're gonna pick on a dead person,
The one dead person you don't pick.
I'll have to convince her she's dead.
But even in real life, she'd harness the powers of the dark side.
I know. She liked the dark side. That was her favourite. She's getting on our backs. Don't get me started on that.
Oh, goodness me, it's just nothing but innuendo and libel.
Dusty Springfield! I don't believe it.
Play— It's libel. Play a record, Gervais.
Oh, God. You should've picked someone like Cilla, who is dead.
Muff Shandy says, "Turn it up." Earplugs Are Gay.
The new single by Muff Shandy. Earplugs Are Gay. Earplugs Are Gay.
And the bloke with the, um, the gimp mask and the umbrella said, "Doris, I'm— even I'm not doing that." And he left.
Gervais, we're leaving it. We're leaving it.

...was talking to my parents on the phone the other day, and, uh, I started swearing. And I've never done this before, and it's a terrible thing 'cause it's— I've crossed this barrier now. I've crossed this line—
—which I previously, for twenty-three-odd years, I'd managed to sort of stay the right side of.
I'm talking to my mum, and she mentions to me that I'm going to lose a lot of money. I don't want to go into it, but I'm going to lose a lot of money. And, um, and she told me how much.
It was, you know, five thousand pounds or something. She went, uh, I went, effing hell. Obviously, I said the real thing. Yeah. Effing hell. She just stopped. She just went, pardon me?
And I thought, what have I done? I thought, I can't explain myself, 'cause she didn't, she didn't know that I knew those words. So I just said, uh, "Well... that's a lot of money."
That got you out of it.
That got me out of it.
But do you know what I mean? That crossing that step.
It's quite a terrible thing. It's like, I, I mean, I, I look forward to the day when I can bring a girl home and say, "Look, I do know about sex."
But what was— what was this all about?
What I was actually gonna say is, um, I don't know if I can say the word "twat".
But, um, when I was a kid and I first went to, to senior school, I started to learn all these swear words that I didn't know—
Of course you can say the word twat.
I started learning all these swear words and I went home and I started using the word twat. I just thought it was a slightly stronger version of twit.
It's a bit tougher for some reason.
And so I used to go around saying that, and I'd go, uh, my sister would say, "Stop ruining me Lego," and I'd go, "You twat."
And, um, uh, make your bed, Steve, no, you're a twat, I'd say to my mum, right? And I didn't realise what it meant.

And my dad, right, he didn't really know much about swear words, so he started using it as well. He started going, "Oh, you're a twat, Steve," and, um, uh, "Do you want to clean the bath?" "No, you twat." And we just started using it all the time, right?
So then at school, Mark Johnson told me what it mean— meant, right?
Obviously I'm stunned. I'm thinking, I can't go around calling my mum a twat.
So I didn't sta— I just stopped using it.
Like that, just stopped using it. But I didn't, I didn't have the guts to tell my dad what it meant.

So he carries on using it, and to this day, we'll be driving along, he'll say, um, to my mum, "Elaine! Watch where you're going, you twat! You great big twat!" And I just wanna say to him, "Dad, don't say that to my mum," 'cause she knows. Oh, she knows what it means.
But she's not, she's not gonna say to him...
Ron, would you stop saying that word? 'Cause—
Yeah. Same thing happened to me. My dad still says "felch".
Felching, talking of that, right, it's Doris Stokes.
And a big bucket and, like, a weight and...
So they haven't actually told you it's your last show?
Well, they wouldn't though, would they? They'd be mad to.
They usually tell you, sort of, they— when you come off they go, "That was your last show." Know what I mean?
See, I'm annoyed, 'cause if I'd, if I'd known it was the last show I'd have, you know, laid on something special.
Yeah, we could have a nice little buffet, you know. Invite round, invite round all the listeners.
Could have probably squeezed them in the studio, in fact.
Um, got 'em all in, you know. I could've put on something nice, probably like a board game or something special.
We could've... No, that was never gonna happen.
do the jerk. Good advice. See, not—not all rock and roll's just, like, bland nonsense. When in Rome, do the jerk. Shall I give it away, as it's the last show?
Man alive. Yeah? Shall I? What a way to go out. Yeah. Giving away the autobiography of Doris Stokes.
